solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Stuffing, say, grand into Rod's bum

indicators.note: stuffing something means packing it inside another thing, so letters go within letters
putting one thing into another places it inside, completing the stuffing instruction

parts.note: a bar is a rod of metal or wood
e.g., for example, is what 'say' means
G is slang shorthand for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: A crude Private Eye image of someone cramming a thousand pounds into a man called Rod's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: Rod looks like a man's name with a possessive, but it is a metal bar, and the 's simply joins it to the definition. Bum is the American sense of a tramp, not a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A bum, in the American sense, is a tramp or vagrant who cadges money, which is exactly what a beggar does.

clue.text: Found bliss at the works, taking time off

indicators.note: if something works it is operated or worked over, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: three words used as raw letters

explanation.surface: Someone discovers happiness on a works outing, taking a break from the job.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine letters of 'bliss at the' rearrange exactly into ESTABLISH; 'taking time off' only colours the scene of a works outing and adds no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To found a company or institution is to set it up from scratch, a standard synonym pairing of two verbs.

clue.text: Perhaps in Greece, getting end away is common to a particular class

indicators.note: the end is sent away, so the final letter of the phrase is lost
perhaps signals a possible version, so the remaining letters may be arranged differently

parts.note: the two words as raw letters, losing the final E

explanation.surface: A smutty suggestion that getting one's end away (having sex) is common practice in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting one's end away' is British slang for having sex, but here it literally removes the end letter of 'in Greece' before the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Generic describes a feature shared by every member of a genus or kind, rather than belonging to one specimen.

clue.text: (& 18dn.) 'Fund Labour organisation' — heartless cheek! Hardly welcomed by punters

indicators.note: organising means putting things into a new order, so the letters are arranged afresh

parts.note: two words used as raw letters

indicators.note: with the heart removed only the two ends of the word are left

parts.note: only the outside letters of the word survive

explanation.surface: A jibe at a Labour Party fundraising group, calling its appeal sheer cheek that gamblers would not welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour organisation' reads as a party body, but 'organisation' is the rearranging signal acting on 'Fund Labour' plus the shell of 'cheek'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambler on a losing streak suffers a sequence of misfortunes, something no punter is glad to see.

clue.text: Bill's main yen: to get through skirt

indicators.note: the main or principal letter of a word is taken as its leading one

parts.note: the opening letter of the name
Y is the abbreviation for the Japanese yen
to pass an exam is to get through it

explanation.surface: Bill's chief longing is to get under a woman's skirt, in typical Private Eye smut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirt' looks like a garment, or slang for women, but it is the verb meaning to go around something.
explanation.definitionFit: To skirt an obstacle or town is to go around its edge, avoiding it, which is what a bypass does.

clue.text: Coarse space turned over for jail

parts.note: broad humour or accent is coarse

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: room means space, as in room to move

explanation.surface: A rough prison cell searched and turned over by guards.
explanation.walkthrough: BROAD is followed by ROOM written backwards. Broadmoor is a high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire, England, holding dangerous offenders.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadmoor confines criminals, so loosely it serves as an example of a lockup or secure institution where inmates are held.

clue.text: Lance, say the magic word: "crumpet!"

parts.note: a pike is a long-shafted weapon of the lance kind
the permitting word that grants a request, as 'please' does

explanation.surface: Someone named Lance is told to mind his manners and say please before asking for a crumpet, slang for an attractive woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Lance looks like a man's name, but it is an example of a weapon. Crumpet doubles as British slang for sexually attractive women.
explanation.definitionFit: A pikelet is a regional British and Australasian name for a small flat crumpet or griddle pancake, a teatime bread.

clue.text: Deliveryman gets head from sex worker in front of one

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only that is taken

parts.note: opening letter of the word
a worker ant is the crossword's standard worker
a means one

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a delivery driver receiving oral sex from a prostitute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets head' reads as sexual slang, but 'head from' just takes the first letter of 'sex'. Santa delivers presents down chimneys.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Christmas brings presents to every home on Christmas Eve, making him a festive courier of parcels and gifts.

clue.text: I have Romney almost brought back in to perform when Trump does nothing?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so a final letter is cut
these letters are placed in another word, held inside it

parts.note: to execute a task is to perform it
the contraction I've without its apostrophe

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Mitt Romney, US senator, with the last letter of his first name cut

explanation.surface: A political jibe: Mitt Romney is roped in to do the work while Donald Trump idles.
explanation.walkthrough: Romney is the US politician Mitt Romney, so his first name is what is trimmed and turned around before going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Executive time was the White House schedule euphemism for long unstructured blocks when President Trump watched television, tweeted and made calls.

clue.text: see 26ac.
Nixon: "F--k the gutless, wussy 'nearest and dearest'"?

indicators.note: a wuss is weak and feeble, so the letters collapse into a new shape

parts.note: the name as raw letters
the two letters actually printed in the censored word

indicators.note: with the guts removed a word keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: only the outside letters survive

explanation.surface: Richard Nixon, in a foul-mouthed outburst, curses his own spineless relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: The censor's dashes leave just F and K to use; the expletive is pure letters, not a word to define.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearest and dearest is an idiom for one's closest family, and next of kin is the formal term for the closest relatives.

clue.text: (& 12ac.) A close shave for a blatant purveyor of fake news?

definitions.text: A close shave for a blatant purveyor of fake news?

parts.note: surface: a near miss, or literally a very smooth shave of the chin

parts.words: a blatant purveyor of fake news
parts.note: setter's reading: someone shameless in telling untruths, whose smooth-shaved face makes the shameless adjective literal

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that a close shave leaves a face bare, so the shameless fibber is literally bare-faced.
explanation.definitionFit: A shameless teller of untruths who does not even try to hide the deceit is called this, and fake news is a modern form.

clue.text: see 11ac.
Guarded Corbynite source introduced to Ed, tires out

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters fall into another arrangement
a source is where something starts, so the word's opening letter is taken

parts.note: opening letter of the word
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cagey insider from Jeremy Corbyn's camp is introduced to Ed Miliband, who is worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: A Corbynite is a supporter of the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn; Ed suggests Ed Miliband, his predecessor, but supplies only its two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone guarded is careful in speech and keeps secrets, which is what being tactful and circumspect means.

clue.text: Recent rumpy-pumpy with Dan was charming

definitions.note: the answer is a past participle, charmed, rather than a verb phrase

indicators.note: rumpy-pumpy is a romp of tumbling bodies, so the letters roll about into a new order

parts.note: taken as raw letters
taken as raw letters

explanation.surface: Someone's recent fling with a man called Dan was delightful.
explanation.walkthrough: Rumpy-pumpy is jokey British slang for sex; here it tumbles the letters. The definition is a loose fit, since the answer is charmed rather than was charming.
explanation.definitionFit: Entranced means held spellbound, so it amounts to being charmed or enchanted by someone or something.

clue.text: Eye-related work on jerk

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
a tic is an involuntary jerk of a muscle

explanation.surface: An eye operation is carried out on some idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' wants to be a fool, but it is a twitch. Private Eye's own title gives the eye theme an in-joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Optic is an adjective describing anything relating to the eye or to vision, as in the optic nerve.

clue.text: Absolutely infatuated with nuts and balls

parts.note: nuts means mad
in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled from one end

explanation.surface: Someone obsessed with testicles, in typically crude Private Eye style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts and balls' reads as slang for testicles, but nuts means mad and balls makes a cricket over.
explanation.definitionFit: To be mad about a person is an idiom for passionate love or obsession, just like being smitten.

clue.text: After triumphant ejaculation, Brexit 'King' removed dress

parts.note: ha! is a cry of triumph

indicators.note: removed means taken away, so some letters are struck from the word

parts.note: taken as written
rex is Latin for king, as in royal signatures

explanation.surface: After shouting in triumph, a man hailed as the King of Brexit strips off his clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ejaculation' is the old sense of a sudden exclamation, and 'removed' looks like undressing but takes the Latin king out of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is the long robe worn by a monk or nun, so it is a particular type of garment or costume.

clue.text: see 4dn.
"Darn, have to play for the gallery!"

indicators.note: letters at play move freely and so can be rearranged

parts.note: two words used as raw letters

explanation.surface: An exasperated performer complains at having to show off to the cheap seats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play to the gallery' means seek popular approval, but here gallery is the definition and 'to play' rearranges the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A veranda is a roofed open platform along the outside of a house, and a gallery is the American word for one.

clue.text: Not this or that element of Brunei, therefore

indicators.note: an element is a component part, so the letters are a piece of the following words

parts.note: found spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A logician's puzzle about an element of Brunei that is somehow neither one thing nor another.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of Brunei and the start of therefore.
explanation.definitionFit: The word refers to not either of two options, so it rules out both this choice and that one.

clue.text: see 26ac.
Copper's penetration of individual is timed perfectly

indicators.note: penetrating something means going into it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: one means a single individual
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A smutty report of a policeman's intimate encounter, said to have been perfectly timed.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper wants to be a police officer, as British slang has it, but it is the metal's chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who enters on cue arrives at exactly the right moment, so the phrase means at just the right time.

clue.text: see 26ac.
Catty thing's bound to get rid of leader

indicators.note: the leader is the front-runner, so the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: to bound is to bounce or leap

explanation.surface: A spiteful remark is sure to oust whoever is in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catty' suggests spite, but the definition is literal: a cat. 'Bound' wants to mean certain; it is a leap.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard, a big wild animal of the cat family in Central Asia.

clue.text: Cleric Charlotte cosied up to servant

parts.note: Charlotte Church is a Welsh singer
a man is a manservant

explanation.surface: Gossip that a priest's Charlotte got cosy with a household servant.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte Church, a Welsh singer once famous as a child soprano, supplies her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A churchman is a member of the clergy, so the word is a straightforward synonym for priest or minister.

clue.text: (& 9/21/23ac.) Hear from very reliable source: "Enjoy sex, working with proficient, powerful body"

parts.note: slang for having sex
a machine that is on is working
to be proficient at something is to be skilled, the everyday opposite of bad
an official body with power

explanation.surface: A trusted tip-off urges someone to enjoy sex with a skilled, muscular partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Powerful body' wants to be a fit physique, but it is an official organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: To have something on good authority is an idiom for learning it from a trustworthy informant, so it can be believed.

clue.text: Hummed in Greek? Edifying!

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: found spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Was someone humming a tune in Greek, and was it uplifting?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hummed' looks like singing with the mouth closed, but in British slang to hum is to stink.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a hum is a bad smell, so to have hummed means to have stunk or smelled foul.

clue.text: Tearaways lacking head for boobs

indicators.note: without its head a word loses its first letter

parts.note: a tearaway, an unruly youngster, is a little terror

explanation.surface: Reckless youths with no sense going after breasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boobs' wants to be breasts; it is the British sense of blunders.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal British English a boob is a silly blunder, so boobs are slips or mistakes.
